extracted.intended_audience: novelists and fiction writers planning or revising subplots
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for novelists on how to plan, write, and insert a subplot into an existing novel structure so it supports theme and character arc. Focuses on a 20-scene layering method (ten main scenes + ten subplot scenes) and practical steps for drafting and placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill the story jar (prioritize main beats first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with the essential plot developments—the 'big rocks'—before layering in subplots and smaller material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original analogy: 'filling a jar with rocks. You want to put the big rocks in, then the pebbles, then the sand, followed by water.' The recommended workflow is to get the primary/essential scenes solid first, then add the next set of scenes (subplots) to 'fill the story.' This is presented as an alternative to plotting strictly sequentially from the beginning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider adding your subplot later (layer after main outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be logical to work out the ten key main scenes first and then layer the subplot elements afterward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author preference: 'I always have worked out those key scenes first and then filled in around them.' This approach lets you focus on primary plot integrity before folding in subplot complications and ensures the subplot is built to fit the main structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write subplot scenes separately as full scenes (treat as a mini-novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft all subplot scenes in a separate document so you can read them straight through as a coherent mini-story with a beginning, middle, climax, and ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical technique: write the subplot scenes in one document with scene breaks, then read them to check flow, continuity, character arc, and missing pieces. Example: author wrote five full scenes for a story-within-a-story and used that to preserve continuity and achieve intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot scenes must be full scenes, not just short excerpts
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplot should consist of full, detailed scenes rather than merely short excerpts or fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While subplot elements can also appear in small bits of dialogue or thought 'throughout the book,' you still need 'full scenes' for strong subplots. Those full scenes let you build subplot plot, character development, and emotional payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every subplot must serve the main plot and impact the protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot should serve the needs of the main plot and affect the protagonist's journey toward her visible goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit rule: 'every subplot should serve the needs of your main plot and impact the protagonist as she goes after her visible goal for the novel.' If it does not, the subplot will feel confusing or purposeless and should be cut or reworked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot should amplify the novel's themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the subplot so that it amplifies and reinforces the central themes of the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: 'first work out a strong subplot that amplifies the themes of your novel, then create an outline of scenes, then write those scenes.' The subplot should deepen meaning, not merely extend length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot resolution should achieve the protagonist's emotional arc ('essence')
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for the subplot's resolution to be the moment the protagonist 'comes into her essence'—an emotional/cathartic resolution of the character arc which may occur after the main-plot climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author emphasis: 'the resolution of the subplot is the moment when the protagonist comes into her essence.' Example: main plot (police case) resolves earlier, but the subplot (mother-son relationship) resolves after the climax and provides the true emotional payoff and MDQ (moral/meaningful driving question) resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of subplot resolution (often after main-plot climax)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared for the subplot's emotional or inner resolution to occur after the main plot's external climax; the subplot can wrap later in the denouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example mapping: main-plot goal may be sealed at ~70% but 'the actual subplot... doesn't resolve until the end of the novel.' The post advises placing the key subplot resolution scene in the final stages so character transformation is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: End concisely after resolving plot and subplot ('Get in quick; get out quick')
rubrics_metrics.description: After you've resolved both plot and subplot, close the novel efficiently; the final scenes should be short and tie up loose ends without dragging out the ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'Get in quick; get out quick.' Tie up loose ends, bring characters on stage for closure, and optionally use a short epilogue rather than extended denouement. Keep final scenes 'short and sweet.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten key main-plot scene types and approximate positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a canonical set of ten main-plot scenes (setup, turning points, pinch points, twists, midpoint, climax, aftermath) positioned roughly by percent through the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author lists the ten primary scenes and approximate percent positions: #1 Setup; #2 Turning Point #1 (10% inciting incident); #3 Pinch Point #1 (~33%); #4 Twist #1; #5 Midpoint (50%); #6 Pinch Point #2 (~62%); #7 Twist #2; #8 Turning Point #4 (75%); #9 Turning Point #5 (76–99% climax); #10 Aftermath (90–99% denouement). These are presented as a commonly-followed backbone across genres but can be deviated from as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten subplot-scene types mapped to the main-plot scaffold (#11–#20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Layer a second set of ten subplot scenes (#11–#20) that map to or mirror the main plot positions so the subplot rises, peaks, and resolves in concert with the main plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's mapped sequence (with intent): #11 – introduction of subplot; #12 – show how inciting incident affects subplot (mirrors 10%); #13 – new subplot development that mirrors/opposes main plot; #14 – progress with subplot; #15 – subplot tension rising/coming to a head; #16 – subplot developments hit critical mass; #17 – subplot feels at a standstill; #18 – subplot issues seem unresolvable or outwardly resolved but emotionally unresolved; #19 – key scene that resolves the subplot fully (emotional payoff); #20 – final parting shot of subplot result (could merge with #19 or be separate). Percent positions are implied by their mapping to the main ten scenes. The post notes bolded scenes in its example and that scene counts/spacing may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot placement and spacing flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Spacing of subplot scenes need not be uniformly distributed; you can place two subplot scenes back-to-back, leave gaps, or vary frequency depending on the main plot's needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'Play around with this. You might not intersperse each of the second ten scenes (subplot scenes) so evenly in this way.' The core rule is to 'drop in those backstory scenes every so often in key places' and build toward the subplot climax while supporting the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare other scenes to receive subplot inserts (add bridging lines/foreshadowing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When inserting subplot scenes into the main manuscript, you may need to add a few lines or adjustments in surrounding scenes to prepare for them and maintain smooth flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process note: after deciding placement, 'you may need to add a few more [scenes], or add in a few lines here and there in other scenes to prepare for what's to come.' Test placements by reading the combined novel to identify continuity issues or missing beats.
